pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Of these four, which would you move onto a queue and which stays in the request: sending a receipt email, checking a password at login, resizing an uploaded avatar, reserving the last ticket in stock? Then name the three bills the queue sends you.
expected_points: queue the work that is slow, bursty, or independent of the response — receipt email and avatar resize
keep synchronous the work whose answer the caller needs now — password check, and the last-ticket reservation because the caller needs the yes/no
latency: the work is done eventually, not when the response returns
consistency: the caller gets 'accepted', not 'done' — read-your-writes is gone and the API must say so (202 plus a status URL)
complexity: one more system to run, plus a new failure vocabulary — redelivery, duplicates, poison messages

questions.prompt: A consumer charges a card and then crashes before its ack reaches the broker. What does the broker actually know, and what are its options? Use that to contrast at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once.
expected_points: the broker only sees a missing ack; it cannot distinguish 'crashed before the work' from 'crashed after' — that information does not exist on its side
at-most-once = never redeliver, so work can be lost; fine only when a loss is cheaper than a duplicate (metrics sample, presence ping)
at-least-once = redeliver until acked, so work can be duplicated; the default for anything that matters
exactly-once delivery is not a broker setting — the ack can always be lost after the side effect committed
what you can build is exactly-once processing: let the transport duplicate and make duplicates harmless at the consumer

questions.prompt: Walk me through your `Handle`: the two ways to make a consumer idempotent, and why a *failed* attempt must not be recorded as done.
expected_points: naturally idempotent operations — absolute statements ('status is shipped') dedupe themselves, deltas ('increment') do not
a dedupe record — check the processed-messages store by the dedupe key before working, record it after, skip and ack on a duplicate
the key is the broker's message ID only when redelivery is the sole source of duplicates; when a producer can republish the same work, key on the business event ID carried in the payload
acking a duplicate is honest because the work genuinely happened
recording a failed attempt turns the retry you designed for into a permanent skip, and the work never happens
in production the dedupe store is durable and shared by all replicas — ideally committed in the same transaction as the side effect

questions.prompt: Your order service must write the order to its database and publish an `order-placed` event. Why is there no safe ordering of those two writes, and how does the transactional outbox fix it?
expected_points: dual-write problem: DB first then publish loses the event on a crash; publish first then DB tells downstream about an order that never happened
retries do not help — the crash lands between the two writes, with no process alive to retry
the fix is to stop doing two writes: insert the event into an outbox table in the SAME transaction as the state change
a separate relay polls unpublished rows, publishes them, and marks them published
a relay crashing between publish and mark republishes — atomicity bought with duplicates, absorbed by the idempotent consumer
those duplicates are distinct broker messages carrying one business event, so the consumer must dedupe on the event ID in the payload, not on the broker's message ID

questions.prompt: A message with a malformed payload fails on every delivery. Describe what happens without a policy, and the retry/dead-letter policy you would put in place.
expected_points: poison message: deliver, fail, time out, redeliver forever — burning consumer capacity and blocking work behind it
bounded attempts, small (3-5), with backoff between them — attempt six teaches nothing attempt five didn't
dead-letter queue: exhausted messages are parked with their content and delivery history, not deleted (deleting is at-most-once through the back door)
a non-empty DLQ is an alert — each message is work the system promised and didn't do
the payoff of parking is replay after fixing the bug; distinguish failure kinds — nack a downstream timeout and let it use the full budget, dead-letter a validation error on the first attempt

questions.prompt: The visibility timeout is a guess. What goes wrong when it is far too short, and what goes wrong when it is far too long?
expected_points: too short: the broker redelivers a message a healthy consumer is still working on — a duplicate you manufactured yourself
too long: a crashed consumer's messages sit invisible for minutes before anyone retries them, delaying recovery
redelivery also reorders — a returned message joins behind newer ones, so queues are roughly FIFO, not FIFO
strict per-key ordering needs a partitioned log (Kafka-style), not a plain queue

questions.prompt: A colleague says your in-process worker pool already has a queue — it uses a buffered channel. What is a channel missing, and dedupe aside, what does that cost you?
expected_points: a channel receive consumes the value: no ack, so a consumer that crashes after receiving silently loses the work
no redelivery, no visibility timeout, no dead-lettering, no durability — it dies with the process
channels move work between goroutines inside one process; a queue moves work between processes that fail independently
the whole point of the ack is that work survives the death of the worker doing it
